t: #3435 Frequencies of Shortest Supersequences — Subset DP over Letters
o: Every word xy demands an x occurring before some y in the supersequence. Since at most 16 distinct letters appear, the key question is which letters must be printed twice: a letter printed once imposes a strict ordering constraint, while a doubled letter relaxes all constraints pointing at it. In example 1 ("ab","ba") either a or b can be the doubled letter, yielding "aba" and "bab"; in example 2 the self-word "aa" forces a to double. So we must find all minimum-size sets D of doubled letters whose remaining constraints form a DAG.
k: Word xy is satisfied iff first(x) < last(y) in the final string.
If y appears once, every edge u→y forces u before y; edges into doubled letters are free.
Feasibility of a doubling set D ⟺ the graph of edges whose head is outside D is acyclic.
Optimal strings use each letter once or twice, so length = |letters| + |D|.

a.i: First compute g[S] = true iff the subgraph induced by letter set S is acyclic, via the recurrence g[S] = exists v in S with no in-neighbor inside S and g[S\{v}]. A doubling set D is feasible exactly when g[allLetters \ D] holds. Enumerate all 2^k subsets, take the minimum popcount, and emit the frequency vector of every optimal D (each D gives a distinct frequency array).
s: Map the ≤16 letters to bits; build in-mask per letter from the words.
DP g over all subsets to mark acyclic induced subgraphs.
Find the minimum |D| with g[full ^ D]; collect all such D and output count vectors (2 for doubled letters, 1 otherwise).
a.t: O(2^k · k + W) with k ≤ 16 — subset DP dominates, W = number of words

w: The crucial lemma is that only edges landing on singly-printed letters constrain the order, so feasibility reduces to induced-subgraph acyclicity. Watch for self-loop words like "aa": they force that letter into every doubling set. A frequent mistake is emitting only one optimal D — all minimum doubling sets must be returned. Follow-up: reconstruct an actual shortest supersequence by topologically ordering the complement and appending second copies.
